content.text: {"persuasion":"PERSUADED","support_scope":"FULL","rationale":"The entry's core — that the Shadow of Death is Death's outline/boundary, the dark edge of a rival kingdom through whose border-valley the Shepherd leads His people into Christ's kingdom — is carried by the supplied texts read together. Dan 2:35,44 explicitly equates the growing mountain with a kingdom; 1 Sam 17:3 supplies the plain picture of a valley as the low ground between two opposing mountains; Col 1:13 states the two-kingdom transfer in so many words ('delivered us from the power of darkness... translated us into the kingdom of his dear Son'); and the shadow-of-death texts are consistently locative and transitional rather than merely qualitative: Israel dwells in 'the LAND of the shadow of death' (Isa 9:2), sits bound in it and is 'brought OUT' of it (Ps 107:10,14), sits in it awaiting guidance 'into the way of peace' (Luke 1:79), and walks THROUGH — not into — the valley of it (Ps 23:4). The strongest counter, the philological 'deep darkness/mortal peril' reading (tsalmut), explains the gloom but not the persistent domain-and-exodus grammar of these texts, and it must sever the very connection ('death') that the KJV texts, the LXX-derived NT citations (skia thanatou in Luke 1:79), and the compound form all preserve. It also cannot say why deliverance from the shadow of death is repeatedly framed as transfer between rival dominions (Ps 107:14; Col 1:13), which the book's core explains directly. No supplied text is inexplicable on the book's reading, so the comparative verdict goes to the book. Every material assertion printed in the entry is supported: shadow as image/outline (tselem built on tsel, shadow attached to its body), valley as the passage between mountain-kingdoms (1 Sam 17:3 + Dan 2), the through-passage from darkness to light and life (Ps 23:4; Col 1:13; Isa 9:2; Luke 1:78-79), and the inverse pairing with the Shadow of Christ (the Messiah's shadow as the place His people live, Lam 4:20; Hos 14:7; the light/darkness antithesis of Isa 9:2, Luke 1:78-79, Col 1:13).","book_core_identification":"The Shadow of Death is the outline/boundary of Death's kingdom (mountains being kingdoms), and the valley of Psalm 23 is the border passage between two kingdoms through which the Shepherd leads His people out of Death's dominion of darkness into Christ's kingdom of light and life.","book_secondary_elaborations":["A shadow is an image, outline, or boundary of its subject.","A valley is the low passage between two mountain-kingdoms (1 Sam 17:3 pattern).","In Psalm 23 the Shepherd leads His people through that border from Death's kingdom of darkness into Christ's kingdom of light and life.","The Shadow of Death is the inverse of the Shadow of Life, i.e., the Shadow of Christ (cross-referenced as its opposite)."],"unsupported_glossary_assertions":[],"chapter_only_objections":["The chapter's anti-supersessionist reading of Colossians 2:16-17 (feasts as the still-standing shadow of Christ's body) is a broader doctrinal application not asserted in the glossary entry.","The chapter's universal thesis that 'shadow' in Scripture always means shelter (spanning ~80 verses, including tsel-as-defence in Numbers 14:9 and Ecclesiastes 7:12) is chapter-level and broader than the entry.","The chapter's reading of Amos 5:8 ('turneth the shadow of death into the morning') and James 1:17 ('no shadow of turning') as light-behind-the-shadow theology is chapter-only elaboration.","Chapter 39 elsewhere reads valleys as 'those enslaved by the mountains' (the humbled), which sits in mild tension with the entry's valley-as-border-passage; that tension belongs to a chapter-level review.","The tselem/tsel etymological derivation (image built on shade-word) is a chapter-level philological argument offered as evidence, not printed in the entry."],"strongest_counter_interpretation":"The philological consensus reading: the Hebrew underlying 'shadow of death' should be understood (or revocalized, tsalmut) as 'deep darkness' — a superlative for gloom, mortal peril, and extreme danger generally, with no locative or kingdom-boundary structure; Psalm 23:4 then means only that God accompanies the believer through life-threatening darkness, and Isa 9:2 / Luke 1:79 extend the gloom image to spiritual hopelessness dispelled by Christ.","counter_core_identification":"'Shadow of death' denotes intense darkness/mortal peril as a quality of experience — the darkest extremity of danger or despair — not the outline or border of a personified Death's kingdom.","counter_relation_to_book_core":"CONTRADICTS","material_core_denial":"The counter denies that the phrase has any structural, quasi-locative referent: on its reading there is no kingdom of Death whose boundary the shadow marks and no border-valley between rival dominions; the phrase is a poetic intensifier for gloom, so the entry's core identification and the counter cannot both be true of the same referent.","counter_case":["Modern lexica and many critical commentators derive the word from a root meaning 'to be dark' (tsalmut), removing 'death' from the etymology; NRSV renders Psalm 23:4 'the darkest valley'.","Job's poetic parallels (Job 3:5; 12:22; 34:22) and Amos 5:8 pair the word with generic darkness, morning, and gloom rather than with a personified Death.","The pastoral force of Psalm 23:4 (fear, comfort, rod and staff) reads naturally as peril-in-life rather than a cosmological border crossing.","The reading requires no symbolic apparatus (mountain=kingdom, valley=border) beyond the plain sense of darkness imagery."],"book_explanatory_advantages":["It explains the consistently locative grammar of the supplied texts: a LAND of the shadow of death (Isa 9:2), people brought OUT of it (Ps 107:14), sitting IN it awaiting guidance out (Luke 1:79; Ps 107:10), and walking THROUGH its valley (Ps 23:4).","It explains why deliverance from the shadow of death is framed as transfer between two dominions — Col 1:13's 'delivered from the power of darkness... translated into the kingdom of his dear Son' — which the entry maps precisely.","Mountain=kingdom is explicitly defined by Scripture itself in the cited texts (Dan 2:35,44), and 1 Sam 17:3 supplies the exact valley-between-two-mountains picture, so the entry's mechanics rest on stated definitions rather than free association.","It preserves the compound 'shadow of death' as the KJV, LXX, and NT citations (Luke 1:79) actually transmit it, treating the shadow as cast by a real body (Death's dominion), consistent with the demonstrated Hebrew usage of tsel as a body's attached covering/outline.","It unifies the Psalm 23 shepherd text with the prophetic light/darkness strand (Isa 9:2; Luke 1:78-79) under one structure instead of treating them as loosely related applications."],"counter_explanatory_advantages":["It is philologically simpler and matches modern lexical scholarship on tsalmut in at least some Job/Amos contexts.","It requires no symbolic composition (kingdom-mountains, border-valleys) to read Psalm 23:4 devotionally.","It comfortably covers uses where the word is paired with mere darkness (Job 3:5; Amos 5:8)."],"evidence_book_core_cannot_explain":[],"comparative_winner":"BOOK","decisive_sources":["Daniel 2:35, 44 (mountain explicitly = kingdom, defined in-text)","1 Samuel 17:3 (valley as the low passage between two opposing mountains)","Colossians 1:13 (explicit two-kingdom transfer: out of the power of darkness into the kingdom of the Son)","Isaiah 9:2 (dwelling in the LAND of the shadow of death; light shines on it)","Psalm 107:10, 14 (sitting in / brought out of darkness and the shadow of death)","Psalm 23:4 (walking THROUGH the valley of the shadow of death under the Shepherd's guidance)","Luke 1:78-79 (dayspring giving light to those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, guiding into the way of peace)","Chapter 17 (shadow as attached covering/outline of a body; kingdom-shadow scaling in Ezek 31, Dan 4, Mark 4:32; Messiah's shadow in Lam 4:20)"],"unresolved_objections":["The philological possibility that the Hebrew originally read tsalmut ('deep darkness') remains a live scholarly alternative outside the supplied KJV evidence, though it does not better explain the locative and kingdom-transfer texts supplied here.","The label 'Shadow of Life' is a coined glossary term with no verbatim scriptural occurrence, though the entry immediately glosses it as the Shadow of Christ, which the evidence (Lam 4:20; Hos 14:7; Col 1:13 antithesis) supports.","Psalm 23 itself never mentions mountains; the two-kingdom border reading depends on the composed symbol set (Dan 2 + 1 Sam 17:3 + Col 1:13) rather than on the psalm's own vocabulary."],"confidence":"medium"}
